title: A pin can last: four ways to meet it
outcomes: Names the four policies against a pinned knight and recognises the question, ignoring and reserves in play
Recognises the question: a flank pawn push at the pinning bishop
Checks whether the centre can be opened before asking again
Knows that more than one policy is often sound

steps.text: A pin need not be won at once; it can shape an opening. When a bishop pins your knight to the queen, you have four policies: **put the question** (a flank pawn attacks the bishop), **ignore** the pin and play in the centre, **bring up reserves** so the knight is no longer pinned, or **hold the choice** with a useful move and decide later. (No exercise here trains this one.)

steps.caption: Black to move. The bishop on g5 pins the knight on f6 to the queen.

line.say: h6 puts the question: the pawn attacks the bishop.
Bh4 keeps the pin. The bishop has answered the question.

claims.statement: h6 is the only pawn move that attacks the bishop.
The engine's first choice is h6.
The queen stands behind the knight.
The bishop on g5 attacks the knight.
e7 is empty, so the knight is pinned to the queen on d8.

steps.text: *Rule of thumb:* the question is good when the bishop's retreat leaves it few squares and the centre cannot be opened, so the bishop cannot come back to life. It is bad when the centre can open, or when the pawn advance leaves your king facing a break. It does not always win a tempo, and it can weaken the side that asks.

steps.title: The second question: ...g5
steps.prompt: Black has played ...h6 and the bishop has gone to h4. Black now asks again with ...g5. In the second position the white f-pawn stands on f4; in the third, Black's queen is on d7. Predict each time, then check.
In the silent positions, which question did you ask first: 'is the piece pinned to something valuable?' or 'can the centre open if I ask?' Which one did you skip?
